p.x:
Last Friday was Sports Day at Nong's school. All the students were in four teams: red, blue, green and yellow. Nong was in the blue team. In the morning, there were races. Nong ran in the 100-metre race and came second. Her friend Fah won the long jump: she jumped nearly four metres!
In the afternoon, there was a football match between the teachers and the older students. The teachers' coach was the headmaster, and he shouted a lot. The score was 3–3 at half-time, but in the end the students won 5–3. The best player was Mr Chai, the English teacher, who scored all three of the teachers' goals.
At the end of the day, the yellow team was the champion, and the blue team was third. Nong was a bit disappointed, but she says next year the blue team will win!

Two years ago, Dao couldn't run for more than two minutes without stopping. Today she runs 10 km every Sunday morning, and last month she took part in her first race with over 3,000 other runners. "I'm not an athlete," she laughs. "I just wanted to be healthier."
Her secret was a beginner's training plan. For the first few weeks she walked and ran in short intervals, three times a week. She always took ten minutes to warm up, and afterwards she stretched her leg muscles carefully. Slowly, the running sections became longer. "The hardest part wasn't my body, it was my mind," she says. "Some days I really didn't want to go."
At the race, Dao didn't try to compete with the fast runners. Her only goal was to finish. When she crossed the line, hundreds of spectators were cheering, and she received a small medal. "It's the only medal I've ever won," she says, "and I'm never taking it off!" Dao's next goal is a half marathon, and she knows there will be days that feel like a defeat. "That's OK," she says. "Even slow progress is progress."

Few things in sport are as exciting as watching an underdog defeat a famous opponent. When Leicester City, a team that had almost been relegated the year before, won the English Premier League in 2016, even fans of rival clubs celebrated. The bookmakers had given them odds of 5,000 to 1.
Psychologists believe we support underdogs because their stories reflect our own struggles. We admire players who outperform expectations through hard work, stamina and agility rather than money. In contrast, the richest clubs, with the biggest sponsors, can seem less human, and a long rivalry between two giants can feel like a battle between corporations.
Underdog stories also remind us of the spirit of amateur sport, in which people play for love rather than money. That spirit is under pressure. Doping scandals have damaged trust in several sports, and some commentators argue that the huge sums involved in professional tournaments encourage cheating. Even so, moments of genuine sportsmanship, such as a runner stopping to help an injured opponent, still attract more attention online than many victories. Perhaps that tells us what we really value in sport.
